Diagnostics

Source: vignettes/diagnostics.qmd

What can go wrong

inla_vanilla() approximates a posterior in stages, and each stage can fail in its own way. The mode search can stop short. The Gaussian can be a poor centre, so the VB correction moves far. A skew-normal can fail to match the shape of a marginal. And each marginal is fitted to a scan of only \(\pm 4\) posterior SDs around the mode, so whatever lies beyond is extrapolated. A posterior SD in these checks is the Laplace SD at the mode, \(\sqrt{\Sigma_{jj}}\), as in INLAvaan; it is not the SD column of the summary table, which is the skew-normal’s.

Each stage is checked as it runs, at almost no cost: the checks reuse what the fit has already computed. summary() reports every check and flags the values that look off, and diagnostics() returns them as numbers. Most problems also raise one warning at the end of the fit. Printing the fit opens with the log marginal likelihood and whether the fit converged, and ends with a line counting its warnings and one counting the flagged checks, each shown only when there are any, so even a fit run with silent = TRUE shows that something needs a look.

Two of the checks say whether the computation reached its solution: the mode check and the VB check. When both pass, the fit has converged. The others judge how well the approximation fits the posterior, which a converged fit can still do badly.

Check In diagnostics(fit, type = "param") Flagged by summary() Fit-time warning From
Mode mode_shift_sigma above 0.1 SDs the same INLAvaan
VB settled vb_step_sigma above 0.1 SDs the same inlavanilla
Hessian hess_cond (in diagnostics(fit)) above \(10^8\) the same INLAvaan
VB correction vb_shift_sigma above 1 SD the same INLAvaan
Skew-normal fit nmad above 0.1 the same INLAvaan
Unscanned mass unscanned_mass above 0.05 the same INLAvaan
Tails tails heavy the same inlavanilla
Ridge bend ridge_bend above 0.25 nats no inlavanilla
Mean gap mean_gap above 0.1 SDs no inlavanilla

Most of these are the checks of INLAvaan’s diagnostics(), under the same names. Jamil and Rue (2026) use the VB shift and NMAD as fit diagnostics, and the gap between the skew-normal and VB means as an internal check; the mode shift, the Hessian condition number and the unscanned mass come from INLAvaan’s diagnostics(), not from the paper. The levels of those five checks are INLAvaan’s, and the fit-time warning uses its words. The VB settling and tails checks are inlavanilla’s own, and so are the ridge bend and mean gap checks, which only summary() flags. Every level is a package default, chosen so that a healthy fit stays silent, and not a calibrated cut-off: a tripped check is a prompt to look again, and silence is not a certificate of accuracy. In the simulations of Jamil and Rue (2026, Section 4.4), the VB shift and NMAD track the loss of accuracy, and the paper reports a calibration of the expected error against them in its Supplementary Material.

A healthy fit

Poisson counts with a Gamma(2, 1) prior on the rate, on the log scale:

library(inlavanilla)

y <- c(2, 0, 3, 1, 4, 2, 1)
logpost_pois <- function(theta, y) {
  rate <- exp(theta[["log_rate"]])
  sum(dpois(y, rate, log = TRUE)) +
    dgamma(rate, 2, 1, log = TRUE) +
    theta[["log_rate"]] # the Jacobian
}
fit_pois <- inla_vanilla(logpost_pois, c(log_rate = 0), y = y, silent = TRUE)
summary(fit_pois)
#> ── INLAvanilla summary ───────────────────────────────── Skew-normal + VB ──
#> 
#> Log marginal likelihood: -12.354 · Converged in 7 iterations (18ms)
#> Laplace -12.362 + VB term 0.0082
#> 66 logpost calls: mode 6ms, VB 2ms, marginals 5ms
#> 
#> ── Posterior marginals ──
#> 
#>              Mean     SD   2.5%    50%  97.5%   Mode
#> 1 log_rate  0.595  0.263  0.047  0.607  1.078  0.631
#> 
#> ── Diagnostics ──
#> 
#>             VB shift    NMAD  Unscanned  Ridge bend  Mean gap
#> 1 log_rate     -0.13  0.0066    0.00038           0   -0.0016
#> 
#> ✔ Mode found in 7 iterations (Newton step 9.8e-08σ).
#> ✔ VB correction settled in 3 iterations: max shift 0.13σ.
#> ✔ Skew-normal fits: max NMAD 0.0066, unscanned mass 0.00038, ridge bend 0,
#>   mean gap 0.0016σ.

Every check passes. The marginal is mildly skewed (its skew-normal shape alpha, in diagnostics(fit_pois, type = "param"), is about -1.4), the skew-normal matches the scan to within 1% of its peak (NMAD), and its mean agrees with the VB-corrected mean.

The mode, the Hessian and the VB correction

The mode is checked by the Newton step there, in posterior SDs (mode_shift_sigma): how far one step of Newton’s method would still move each parameter. It is flagged above 0.1, INLAvaan’s level, whatever the optimiser’s return code, because without a gradient the optimiser can report failure at an accurate mode, and success short of one. When the mode is off, the warning says so first, and suggests what to change.

hess_cond is the condition number of the Hessian at the mode, with each parameter in posterior-SD units: the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue of the posterior correlation matrix. Above \(10^8\) some combination of the parameters is weakly identified. INLAvaan takes the condition number on the raw scale of the parameters, where a mere change of units can make it large; inlavanilla allows posterior SDs from \(10^{-6}\) to \(10^4\), so it measures it in posterior SDs instead.

The VB correction recentres the Gaussian at the shift that minimises its Kullback-Leibler divergence from the posterior (Jamil & Rue, 2026, Section 3.1). vb_shift_sigma is how far it moved each mean from the mode, in posterior SDs. vb_shift is the same shift on the scale of logpost, and kld, half the square of vb_shift_sigma, is the Kullback-Leibler divergence of each shifted marginal from the unshifted one. A shift of a few tenths is normal for a skewed posterior; a shift above 1 SD means that the posterior is far from the Laplace Gaussian. When the fixed-point iteration hands over to the optimiser, fit$diagnostics$vb records it, and summary() and the verbose output report it, but, as in INLAvaan, it is not flagged: it is a route of the solver, not a sign of a poor approximation.

Where the solver lands is checked as the mode is. vb_step_sigma is the step still to go at the VB mean, in posterior SDs: the fixed-point step there, which is the Newton step of the condition the VB mean solves. Above 0.1, the level of the mode check, the correction has not settled and the fit has not converged. The VB mean is then off, and with it the VB term of the log marginal likelihood and the expansions of loo() and waic(). The skew-normal marginals do not depend on it, since they are scanned around the mode, and vb = FALSE leaves it out. Gaussian marginals (marginals = "gaussian") are centred on it, and vb = FALSE centres them at the mode instead. Without a gradient, the usual cause is not the solver but the VB mean itself: from logpost values alone it is exact only for a log-posterior of degree four, and on a strongly skewed posterior it can be about 0.1 SDs out. Supplying grad is the fix.

With a gradient the fallback takes one more step of its own. If it lands short of settled, it is run once more from where it landed, much as the mode search reruns its optimiser when the gradient at the mode is not yet small. This can happen when the optimiser starts where a node fails: the lowest node around the mode sits on a boundary of the support, say, so its first value is a failure, and it then reports convergence too early. The rerun costs nothing when the first run settles, and one more run of the optimiser when it does not. It is not a check, so summary() does not mention it, but verbose = TRUE reports it: “Fell back to nlminb, as …, rerun once from where it landed”. Without a gradient no rerun is made, since its optimiser is steered by the same estimate of the expected gradient and cannot settle any closer.

The skew-normal mean and the VB mean both estimate the posterior mean, by different routes. Both recover the leading, \(O(n^{-1})\) shift from the mode to the mean, so they agree to \(O(n^{-2})\) (Jamil & Rue, 2026, Proposition 3.4). mean_gap is their gap in posterior SDs. A gap signals that the higher-order terms of that expansion about the mode matter, or numerical error (Section 5.1), and a gap above 0.1 is flagged.

The skew-normal fit

nmad is the largest gap between the fitted skew-normal and the scanned log-posterior, on the density scale and relative to the peak (Jamil & Rue, 2026, Section 4.4). A skew-normal has one mode and one direction of skew, so it cannot follow a marginal with two bumps:

logpost_mix <- function(theta) {
  log(0.7 * dnorm(theta[[1]], 0, 1) + 0.3 * dnorm(theta[[1]], 3, 1))
}
fit_mix <- inla_vanilla(logpost_mix, c(theta = -0.2))
#> ✔ Found the posterior mode in 4 iterations [5ms]
#> ✔ VB mean correction, max shift 0.39σ [14ms]
#> ✔ Fitted 1 skew-normal marginal [3ms]
#> Warning: Fit diagnostics flagged 3 potential issues:
#> ✖ The fitted marginal deviates from the scanned posterior (NMAD > 0.1) for
#>   `theta` (0.20).
#> ✖ The fitted marginal puts more than 0.05 of its mass beyond the scanned
#>   window (4σ either side of the mode) for `theta` (0.09); its credible
#>   limits rely on extrapolation.
#> ✖ Heavy tails for `theta`: the density is still over 5% of its peak at the
#>   ends of the scanned window (4σ either side of the mode), and the
#>   skew-normal extrapolates beyond it.
#> ℹ Inspect with `diagnostics(fit)` and `diagnostics(fit, type = "param")`;
#>   `vignette("diagnostics", package = "inlavanilla")` explains each check.

The fit ends with one warning that lists every problem. The second bump puts mass far beyond what the Laplace SD expects, so the skew-normal fits the scan poorly, it stretches its own tail out of the scanned window to cover the bump, and the tails are heavy. diagnostics() gives the numbers behind the warning, for the whole fit and for each parameter:

diagnostics(fit_mix)
#>               npar          converged         iterations           grad_inf 
#>                  1                  1                  4           1.99e-08 
#>       grad_inf_rel            grad_l2     mode_shift_max          hess_cond 
#>           4.78e-08           1.99e-08           2.04e-08           1.00e+00 
#>         vb_applied       vb_shift_max      vb_kld_global            kld_max 
#>                  1             0.3921             0.0769             0.0769 
#>           kld_mean           nmad_max          nmad_mean unscanned_mass_max 
#>             0.0769             0.1963             0.1963           9.13e-02 
#>        vb_fallback        vb_step_max       mean_gap_max     ridge_bend_max 
#>                  0           6.87e-04             0.7627             0.0000 
#>      n_heavy_tails 
#>                  1
diagnostics(fit_mix, type = "param")
#>   names grad grad_abs grad_rel mode_shift_sigma    kld vb_shift
#> 1 theta    0        0        0                0 0.0769   0.4011
#>   vb_shift_sigma   nmad alpha unscanned_mass vb_step_sigma mean_gap gamma1
#> 1         0.3921 0.1963 4.546         0.0913         7e-04   0.7627      0
#>   tails ridge_bend
#> 1 FALSE          0

plot(type = "sn_fit") shows the fit against the scan it was fitted to, as INLAvaan’s plot of the same name does: on the scan coordinate, in posterior SDs from the mode, the log-posterior along the scan (“Raw”), the same with the volume correction added (“Corrected”), and the fitted skew-normal. NMAD is the largest gap between the last two. type = "sn_fit_log" draws the same on a log scale.

plot(fit_mix, type = "sn_fit")

Against the exact density, the skew-normal covers both modes but follows neither:

# The skew-normal density, from the fit's xi, omega and alpha
dskewnorm <- function(x, xi, omega, alpha) {
  z <- (x - xi) / omega
  2 / omega * dnorm(z) * pnorm(alpha * z)
}
theta <- seq(-4, 7, length.out = 400)
exact <- 0.7 * dnorm(theta, 0, 1) + 0.3 * dnorm(theta, 3, 1)
sn <- fit_mix$sn[1, ]
fitted <- dskewnorm(theta, sn[["xi"]], sn[["omega"]], sn[["alpha"]])
par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(
  theta, exact, type = "l", lwd = 2, las = 1, bty = "n",
  xlab = "theta", ylab = "density", ylim = c(0, 0.33)
)
lines(theta, fitted, col = "#eb6834", lwd = 2)
legend(
  "topright", c("exact", "skew-normal fit"),
  col = c("black", "#eb6834"), lwd = 2, bty = "n"
)

Ridge bend

Each marginal is scanned along a straight line through the mode, the conditional mode path (CMP) on which the Laplace Gaussian puts the other parameters at their conditional mode given this one (Jamil & Rue, 2026, Lemma 3.1). The straight line is a first-order approximation to a possibly curved ridge of high posterior density (Section 3.2.1). When the ridge bends away from the CMP, the scan misses log-density, and the marginal comes out too narrow. The ridge bend, ridge_bend, inlavanilla’s own check, is the log-density, in nats, that one Newton step in the other parameters would recover at \(\pm 2\) posterior SDs.

This happens when a parameter’s spread depends on another parameter that the data pin down poorly. A normal mean with an unknown SD, from 12 observations, is the textbook case:

set.seed(4)
y12 <- rnorm(12, 10, 2)
logpost_norm <- function(theta, y) {
  sum(dnorm(y, theta[["mu"]], exp(theta[["log_sigma"]]), log = TRUE)) +
    dnorm(theta[["mu"]], 0, 100, log = TRUE) +
    dnorm(theta[["log_sigma"]], 0, 10, log = TRUE)
}
fit_norm <- inla_vanilla(
  logpost_norm, c(mu = 9, log_sigma = 0.5), y = y12, silent = TRUE
)
signif(fit_norm$diagnostics$marginals[, c("nmad", "ridge_bend")], 2)
#>              nmad ridge_bend
#> mu        1.9e-06    3.3e-01
#> log_sigma 1.1e-02    4.9e-07

summary() flags the ridge bend of mu. The exact marginal SD of mu, from a grid, shows how much narrower the skew-normal is:

grid <- expand.grid(
  mu = seq(7, 15, length.out = 401),
  log_sigma = seq(-1, 2.5, length.out = 401)
)
lp <- apply(grid, 1, function(g) logpost_norm(g, y12))
w <- exp(lp - max(lp))
w <- w / sum(w)
m <- sum(w * grid$mu)
sds <- c(
  exact = sqrt(sum(w * (grid$mu - m)^2)),
  skew_normal = fit_norm$summary["mu", "SD"]
)
sds
#>       exact skew_normal 
#>   0.6125832   0.5308595

The skew-normal SD of mu is 13% too small here. The gap shrinks as \(1/n\): for a normal mean with an unknown SD it is about 3% at 50 observations and under 1% at 200. For this model the ridge bend \(b\) gives the gap: the SD is too small by \(1 - \sqrt{1 - 3b/4}\), roughly \(3b/8\), and \(b\) is close to \(4/n\). From its ridge bend of 0.33, the formula gives 13%. summary() flags a ridge bend above 0.25, where the formula gives 10%. In other models it is a rough guide to how much: on test models it was mostly within a factor of 1.5 of the true gap, and it overstated the narrowing in logistic and Poisson regressions.

Tails and unscanned mass

Both checks are about the edge of the scanned window, but they look at different things:

  • tails reads the log-posterior itself at the two ends of the scan. It is flagged when either end is still within 3 nats of the peak, that is, when the density there is over 5% of its peak. A Gaussian is 8 nats down at \(\pm 4\) SDs.
  • unscanned_mass is the mass the fitted skew-normal puts beyond the window, where it is extrapolated (as INLAvaan’s diagnostics() reports it). A Gaussian marginal gives \(2\Phi(-4) = 6.3 \times 10^{-5}\); the larger it is, the more of the marginal is extrapolated.

Neither one can see the mass the true posterior has beyond the window. The figure shows three one-parameter posteriors whose exact densities are known. The x axis is in posterior SDs from the mode, so the scanned window is always \(-4\) to \(4\) (the grey band).

In the top row, tails reads the open circles against the dashed line 3 nats below the peak. In the bottom row, the orange shading is unscanned_mass and the grey shading is the exact posterior’s mass beyond the window.

  1. Well behaved. The scan ends are 5.8 and 11.6 nats down, either side of a Gaussian’s 8, as the Poisson log rate is a little skewed, and neither the fit nor the posterior has much mass outside. Both checks are rightly quiet.
  2. Heavy inside the window. A Cauchy posterior is still high at the ends of the scan, so tails fires, and the fit warns. unscanned_mass stays under 0.05: the skew-normal has Gaussian tails, so whatever it fits, it puts little mass outside the window. It exceeds 0.05 only when the fit itself is very wide or very skewed, as for the mixture above.
  3. Heavy beyond the window. Here the data can only bound a variance from above, so its log has a long left tail that only the prior holds back. The tail flattens out beyond the window: the scan end is already more than 3 nats down, and the skew-normal puts little mass outside. Both checks are quiet, but the exact posterior has 0.025 of its mass outside, against 0.006 for the fit.

The third case is the known limit of a skew-normal at a boundary: no check that reads only the scanned window can see a tail that starts beyond it. Jamil and Rue (2026, Section 4.4) find the same miss in the lower tail of a variance near zero, the boundary pile-up that a unimodal skew-normal cannot capture. In the structural equation model of the Rcpp article, two log residual variances behave like this, more strongly. Their skew-normal marginals are too narrow on the log scale, although on the variance scale the error is much smaller. INLAvaan gives the same marginals there.

The warning

The fit-time warning is a condition of class inlavanilla_diagnostics_warning, which is also an inlavanilla_warning. Its headline counts the problems, as INLAvaan’s does, and it names at most three parameters for each; summary() lists them all. With silent = TRUE nothing is printed, and every warning raised during the fit is kept in fit$warnings as plain text, a line per bullet with no wrapping, which suits simulations. Here it is wrapped to fit the page:

fit_mix_quiet <- inla_vanilla(logpost_mix, c(theta = -0.2), silent = TRUE)
length(fit_mix_quiet$warnings)
#> [1] 1
bullets <- strsplit(fit_mix_quiet$warnings, "\n")[[1]]
writeLines(strwrap(bullets, width = 76, exdent = 2))
#> Fit diagnostics flagged 3 potential issues:
#> ✖ The fitted marginal deviates from the scanned posterior (NMAD > 0.1) for
#>   `theta` (0.20).
#> ✖ The fitted marginal puts more than 0.05 of its mass beyond the scanned
#>   window (4σ either side of the mode) for `theta` (0.09); its credible
#>   limits rely on extrapolation.
#> ✖ Heavy tails for `theta`: the density is still over 5% of its peak at the
#>   ends of the scanned window (4σ either side of the mode), and the
#>   skew-normal extrapolates beyond it.
#> ℹ Inspect with `diagnostics(fit)` and `diagnostics(fit, type = "param")`;
#>   `vignette("diagnostics", package = "inlavanilla")` explains each check.

To handle the warning in code, catch its class:

fit <- withCallingHandlers(
  inla_vanilla(logpost_mix, c(theta = -0.2)),
  inlavanilla_diagnostics_warning = function(w) {
    message("Check this fit.")
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
#> ✔ Found the posterior mode in 4 iterations [1ms]
#> ✔ VB mean correction, max shift 0.39σ [1ms]
#> ✔ Fitted 1 skew-normal marginal [3ms]
#> Check this fit.

Checks on a supplied gradient

When you pass grad, it is compared with finite differences of logpost at init, per posterior SD, and its Jacobian at the mode is checked for symmetry, as the Hessian of a function must be. Either failure gives a warning of its own, because a wrong gradient gives a wrong mode and wrong marginals.

References

Jamil, H., & Rue, H. (2026). Approximate Bayesian inference for structural equation models using integrated nested Laplace approximations (arXiv:2603.25690 [stat.ME]). arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.25690
